name: Cheatcode for SAA. Service to trigger words
source: Hand-curated cheatcode deck. Each card is one AWS service with 3-5 abstract, distinctive trigger keywords that signal this service in an SAA-C03 question stem. Built for last-minute spot-the-service drilling.

cards.a:
• full OS control
• long-running compute
• lift-and-shift VM workloads

• fault-tolerant
• interruptible
• up to 90% cheaper
• stateless batch
cards.explanation: 'Stateless batch' = a job that doesn't depend on prior runs and can restart anywhere (image processing, ML training, CI/CD). Spot can be reclaimed with a 2-minute notice.

cards.a:
• 1 or 3 year commitment
• steady predictable workload
• specific instance family

• 1 or 3 year commitment
• flexible across families and Regions
• best across Lambda/Fargate/EC2
cards.explanation: Commit to $X/hour of compute spend for 1 or 3 years; AWS automatically applies the discount to EC2, Fargate, and Lambda usage across families and Regions. Most flexible commitment.

cards.a:
• guaranteed capacity in a Region/AZ
• no commitment
• DR failover Region

• preserve RAM state
• long boot apps
• warm pool

• low-latency between instances
• HPC
• tight network coupling
cards.explanation: Instances are packed close in the same AZ for high-throughput, low-latency networking, ideal for HPC and tightly-coupled workloads.

cards.a:
• instances on different hardware
• small fleet HA
• avoid single hardware failure
cards.explanation: Each instance is on distinct underlying hardware (rack), so a single hardware failure can take down at most one instance in the group. Limited to 7 instances per AZ.

cards.a:
• large distributed workloads
• Hadoop/Cassandra
• fault isolation per partition
cards.explanation: Instances are split into logical partitions, each on separate hardware. Made for distributed/replicated systems like Hadoop, Cassandra, Kafka where each partition tolerates a hardware failure.

cards.a:
• single-digit ms latency to a metro area
• extend VPC to a city
• compliance forces local hosting
cards.explanation: Extension of an AWS Region into a metropolitan area for single-digit-ms latency to local users. The VPC is stretched. Use when compliance forces local hosting but you still want managed AWS services.
tricks: single-digit ms latency to a metro area

cards.a:
• 5G mobile carrier
• ultra-low latency to mobile users
• telco edge
cards.explanation: AWS infrastructure deployed inside 5G telecom carrier networks. Used for ultra-low-latency mobile apps (gaming, AR/VR, autonomous vehicles).

cards.a:
• AWS hardware on-prem
• compliance keeps data local
• consistent AWS services on-prem
cards.explanation: Physical AWS-managed rack installed in the customer's data center. Customer is responsible for power, network, and physical security; AWS owns the hardware lifecycle.

cards.a:
• short stateless code
• event-driven
• scales to thousands instantly
• per-request billing

• expose Lambda as HTTPS
• no API Gateway needed
• simple webhook

• reduce Java cold starts
• free
• JVM snapshot resume
cards.explanation: Snapshots the JVM right after init and resumes from the snapshot at invocation, killing most of the cold-start latency for Java. Free, only available for Java for now.

cards.a:
• pre-warmed Lambda
• predictable low latency
• scheduled scaling for known peaks
cards.explanation: Pre-warmed Lambda containers always ready to serve, eliminating cold starts. Costs extra (you pay for the warm instances). Use for predictable peaks (e.g. business hours).

cards.a:
• containers without managing servers
• no EC2 patching
• pay per task
cards.explanation: Run containers without managing EC2 nodes. AWS handles the host. You pay per task (vCPU and memory), no patching needed.

cards.a:
• managed Kubernetes
• K8s API compatibility
• hybrid Kubernetes via EKS Anywhere

• push container, get URL
• auto-scale web app
• no infra config

• orchestrate multi-step workflow
• visual state machine
• error/retry/parallel built in

• parallel process thousands of S3 items
• serverless
• no orchestration code
cards.explanation: The Map state in 'Distributed' mode can fan-out thousands of S3 objects in parallel, far beyond Inline Map's 40-iteration cap. Use for parallel batch processing of large datasets without writing orchestration code.
tricks: parallel process thousands of S3 items

cards.a:
• single-instance block storage
• persistent
• SSD or HDD volume

• default block storage
• decouple IOPS from size
• cheaper than gp2
cards.explanation: General purpose SSD with IOPS and throughput priced separately from size. Default since 2021, cheaper than gp2 for most workloads.

cards.a:
• latency-sensitive databases
• consistent high IOPS
• mission-critical workloads
cards.explanation: SSD where you provision IOPS independently and get sub-millisecond latency with 99.999% durability for io2 Block Express. Use for the most demanding databases.

cards.a:
• one volume to multiple EC2
• io1/io2 only
• same AZ
cards.explanation: Same EBS volume attached to multiple EC2 in the same AZ at the same time. Limited to io1/io2 SSDs. App must handle concurrent writes (cluster-aware filesystem).

cards.a:
• lowest latency block
• ephemeral
• data lost on stop
cards.explanation: NVMe SSD physically attached to the host. Lowest latency you can get on AWS, but data is lost when the instance stops or terminates. Pure scratch space.

cards.a:
• NFS shared file system
• multiple Linux EC2 across AZs
• elastic capacity
cards.explanation: Fully-managed NFS v4 shared filesystem. Mounted simultaneously from many Linux EC2s across AZs. Storage is elastic (no capacity planning).

cards.a:
• SMB share
• Active Directory integration
• Windows file workloads

• HPC parallel file system
• sub-millisecond
• S3 link
cards.explanation: Parallel filesystem optimized for HPC and ML training. Sub-ms latency, hundreds of GB/s throughput. Can sync to/from an S3 bucket so you process data with Lustre and persist to S3.

cards.a:
• multi-protocol NFS + SMB
• SnapMirror replication
• ONTAP features
cards.explanation: Multi-protocol filesystem (NFS, SMB, iSCSI) with NetApp ONTAP features (snapshots, SnapMirror replication, dedup). Used to lift-and-shift NetApp workloads to AWS.

cards.a:
• object storage
• 11 nines durability
• static website hosting
• data lake

• infrequent access
• multi-AZ resilient
• retrieval fee
cards.explanation: Same durability and AZ-resilience as Standard but cheaper per-GB. Charged a small retrieval fee per request, so worth it only if access frequency is below ~1/month.

cards.a:
• single AZ
• re-creatable data
• cheaper than Standard-IA
cards.explanation: Stored in a single AZ. Cheapest non-archive class but data is lost if that AZ is destroyed. Only for re-creatable data (thumbnails, secondary copies).

cards.a:
• unpredictable access pattern
• auto-tier
• no retrieval fee
cards.explanation: S3 monitors access patterns per object and moves it between frequent and infrequent tiers automatically. No retrieval fee. Use when access patterns are unpredictable.

cards.a:
• archive but retrieved instantly
• ms latency
• rarely accessed

• minutes to hours retrieval
• cheap archive
• tape replacement

• 12+ hour retrieval
• cheapest archive
• long-term compliance
cards.explanation: Cheapest AWS storage class. Retrieval takes 12+ hours. Use for compliance archive kept for years and almost never read.

cards.a:
• global users uploading to one bucket
• CloudFront edge upload
• long-distance transfer
cards.explanation: Uploads go to the closest CloudFront edge location and ride the AWS backbone to the destination bucket. Speeds up long-distance uploads to a single bucket from global users.
tricks: global users uploading to one bucket

cards.a:
• auto-copy new objects to another Region
• compliance
• DR
tricks: auto-copy new objects to another Region

cards.a:
• transition between storage classes
• expire old objects
• automate tiering

• WORM
• prevent deletion or modification
• regulatory compliance
cards.explanation: WORM = Write Once Read Many. Once written, an object cannot be deleted or overwritten for the retention period. Required for SEC 17a-4 / FINRA / HIPAA compliance use cases.

cards.a:
• nobody can delete (not even root)
• fixed retention
• strict immutability
cards.explanation: Strictest WORM mode: not even the AWS root user can shorten retention or delete the object. Used when regulators require provable immutability.

cards.a:
• protect against accidental deletion
• MFA required to delete versions
• rollback to old versions
cards.explanation: Versioning keeps every version of each object. MFA Delete forces a hardware MFA token to permanently delete a version. Together they protect against accidental or malicious deletes.

cards.a:
• temporary upload/download permission
• browser direct to S3
• time-limited access

• on-prem NFS/SMB to S3
• local cache for hot files
• extend on-prem storage

• org-wide S3 visibility
• incomplete multipart upload report
• storage analytics

• replace on-prem iSCSI block storage
• cached or stored mode
• S3-backed
cards.explanation: Exposes iSCSI block volumes to on-prem servers, backed by S3. 'Cached' mode keeps frequently used data on-prem; 'Stored' mode keeps the full dataset on-prem and async backs it up to S3.

cards.a:
• replace physical tape backups
• iSCSI VTL
• existing backup software
cards.explanation: Emulates a Virtual Tape Library over iSCSI. Existing on-prem backup software (Veeam, Veritas, Commvault) sees it as physical tape. Tapes are stored on S3 and Glacier.

cards.a:
• managed relational DB
• MySQL/Postgres/Oracle/SQL Server
• patching/backup automated

• synchronous standby in another AZ
• automatic failover
• high availability for RDS
cards.explanation: Synchronous standby in a different AZ. Automatic failover (~60-120s) on primary failure. Standby is NOT readable in instance deployment (use Multi-AZ DB cluster for readable standbys).

cards.a:
• 1 writer + 2 readable standbys
• faster failover
• read scaling + HA
cards.explanation: Newer Multi-AZ flavor: 1 writer + 2 standby readers across 3 AZs. Failover in seconds, and the standbys are readable so you get HA + read scaling.

cards.a:
• connection pooling for RDS/Aurora
• Lambda connection storms
• reduce failover downtime
cards.explanation: Connection pool in front of RDS/Aurora. Solves Lambda 'connection storms' and reduces failover downtime perceived by the app.

cards.a:
• test new version safely
• near-zero downtime upgrade
• auto-rollback
cards.explanation: Spin up a parallel green environment at the new version, test, then atomically switch traffic. Near-zero downtime upgrade with rollback if it goes wrong.

cards.a:
• offload read queries
• async replication
• scale reads only
cards.explanation: Asynchronous replica used to offload read queries from the primary. Eventual consistency. Can be promoted to standalone DB if needed.

cards.a:
• MySQL/Postgres compatible
• 5x faster than RDS
• auto-scaling storage

• sub-10ms reader replication
• shared storage
• auto-scale readers

• multi-Region writer + replicas
• sub-second cross-Region replication
• DR with promote
cards.explanation: Single Aurora cluster with one writer Region and up to 5 reader Regions. Sub-second cross-Region replication, RPO close to zero. Used for global apps and multi-Region DR.

cards.a:
• auto-scale capacity in seconds
• intermittent or unpredictable load
• scale near zero when idle
cards.explanation: Aurora capacity (ACUs) auto-scales in seconds based on load, can scale near zero when idle. Use for unpredictable or intermittent workloads (dev environments, end-of-month batch).

cards.a:
• NoSQL key-value
• single-digit ms latency
• any scale

• unpredictable traffic
• pay per request
• no capacity planning
cards.explanation: Pay per request, no capacity to plan. Best when traffic is unpredictable, spiky, or you don't know the load yet. More expensive than Provisioned at high steady throughput.

cards.a:
• known steady throughput
• cheaper at high RCU/WCU
• auto-scaling

• multi-Region active-active writes
• eventual consistency
• multi-master
cards.explanation: Multi-Region active-active replication. Each Region has a writer; conflicts resolved by last-writer-wins. Eventual consistency across Regions.

cards.a:
• change data capture
• trigger Lambda on item change
• downstream replication
cards.explanation: CDC = Change Data Capture. Every item change emits an event you can consume from Lambda or Kinesis. Used for cross-Region replication, search index sync, audit log.

cards.a:
• DynamoDB cache
• ms to microsecond latency
• transparent client
• no app code change
cards.explanation: DynamoDB Accelerator. In-memory cache that talks the DynamoDB API. Drops read latency from ms to microseconds. Transparent to the app: same SDK, no code change.

cards.a:
• distributed session state
• persistence + replication
• Multi-AZ
cards.explanation: In-memory store with replication, persistence (AOF/RDB), and Multi-AZ failover. Used for session state, leaderboards, caches that must survive node failure.

cards.a:
• simple in-memory cache
• no persistence
• horizontal scaling
cards.explanation: Pure in-memory cache. No replication, no persistence, no failover. Lost on node failure. Use only when cached data is recomputable.

cards.a:
• graph database
• social network / fraud / recommendations
• Gremlin or SPARQL
cards.explanation: Managed graph database. Stores nodes and edges. Used for social graphs, fraud detection, recommendations, knowledge graphs.

cards.a:
• data warehouse
• petabyte SQL analytics
• columnar storage

• search and log analytics
• near real-time indexing
• Kibana dashboards

• 1:1 between two VPCs
• free same-Region
• no overlapping CIDRs

• hub-and-spoke
• hundreds of VPCs
• central routing

• dedicated private line
• consistent low latency
• high bandwidth hybrid

• IPsec over internet
• quick to set up
• DC backup

• private access to AWS or 3rd-party services
• no internet/NAT/peering
• interface endpoint
cards.explanation: Private connectivity from your VPC to AWS or third-party services without going over the internet. Implemented as Interface VPC Endpoints (one ENI per AZ).
tricks: private access to AWS or 3rd-party services

cards.a:
• private access to S3 or DynamoDB
• free
• route table entry only
cards.explanation: Free private route from VPC to S3 or DynamoDB only (no other AWS service). Implemented via the VPC route table, not an ENI. Use this to remove S3/DynamoDB traffic from the NAT.
tricks: private access to S3 or DynamoDB

cards.a:
• private access to AWS services other than S3/DynamoDB
• ENI per AZ
• DNS in VPC
cards.explanation: Private access to most AWS services other than S3/DynamoDB, via an ENI in your subnets. You pay per AZ-hour and per GB processed.
tricks: private access to AWS services other than S3/DynamoDB

cards.a:
• private subnet outbound to internet
• managed
• per-GB processing fee
cards.explanation: Managed outbound internet for private subnets. Auto-scaled, HA per AZ. Costs both per-hour and per-GB processed (S3/DynamoDB traffic via NAT is wasteful, use a Gateway Endpoint instead).

cards.a:
• HTTP/HTTPS
• path/host-based routing
• WebSocket and HTTP/2
• Layer 7

• TCP/UDP
• ultra-low latency
• millions of connections
• Layer 4
cards.explanation: Layer 4 (TCP/UDP). Lowest latency, handles millions of connections per second. Use for TCP/UDP non-HTTP workloads, gaming, IoT.

cards.a:
• transparent inline traffic inspection
• third-party firewall/IPS
• GWLB endpoint
cards.explanation: Transparent traffic insertion: incoming traffic is routed through third-party network appliances (firewall, IPS, DPI) before reaching the destination. Uses GWLB endpoints in your VPCs.

cards.a:
• CDN edge cache
• HTTPS for global users
• DDoS protection
• S3 origin

• per-user access to one file
• movie rental / song download
• time-limited
cards.explanation: Per-user URL granting access to one specific object for a limited time. Used for movie rentals, paywalled downloads, time-boxed access.

cards.a:
• allow or block by country
• content licensing rights
• edge enforcement

• primary/secondary endpoints
• health-check based
• active-passive

• route by user country
• regional content rights
• data residency

• closest Region by latency
• global users
• no health-check failover
cards.explanation: Each user is routed to the Region with lowest network latency from their location. Pure performance optimization, not health-aware (combine with health checks for failover).

cards.a:
• A/B testing
• blue/green deployment
• traffic split by weight

• UDP and TCP non-HTTP traffic
• anycast IPs
• fast multi-Region failover
• AWS backbone
cards.explanation: Anycast IPs (2 static IPs). Traffic enters the AWS backbone at the closest edge location, then takes the AWS internal network to the healthy Region. Cross-Region failover in seconds, beats Route 53 DNS-based failover for live UDP/TCP traffic.

cards.a:
• REST/HTTP/WebSocket APIs
• authorizers
• throttling
• fully managed

• decouple producer and consumer
• buffer spikes
• at-least-once delivery

• exactly-once
• preserve order
• 300 messages/s default
cards.explanation: Exactly-once processing and strict ordering within a message group. Lower throughput than Standard (300 msg/s without batching). Use when order or deduplication matters.

cards.a:
• pub/sub topic
• fan-out to many subscribers
• push to email/SMS/HTTP

• one event, many independent consumers
• durable per-consumer queue
• decoupled processing rate
cards.explanation: Common pattern: one SNS topic publishes once, multiple SQS queues subscribe. Each consumer reads its own queue at its own pace, with retries and DLQ. Decouples one producer from many consumers.

cards.a:
• event bus
• SaaS event integration
• rule-based routing
cards.explanation: Serverless event bus. Receives events from AWS services, your apps, and 100+ SaaS partners. Rules route events to targets (Lambda, SQS, Step Functions, etc.).

cards.a:
• TB to PB offline transfer
• low bandwidth or no internet
• physical device shipped

• small site / edge
• 8-14 TB
• rugged portable device

• one-time or scheduled file copy
• auto integrity check
• on-prem NFS/SMB to AWS

• heterogeneous DB migration
• ongoing CDC replication
• SCT for schema conversion
cards.explanation: Migrates databases between heterogeneous engines (Oracle to Aurora, SQL Server to RDS, etc.). Supports continuous CDC replication for near-zero-downtime migrations. Combine with Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) for schema changes.

cards.a:
• managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP
• users land files in S3 or EFS
• no servers to manage
tricks: users land files in S3 or EFS

cards.a:
• block-level replication from on-prem
• pilot light DR to AWS
• RPO seconds
cards.explanation: Block-level replication of on-prem servers (or another cloud) to AWS. RPO measured in seconds. Used as a pilot-light DR target: replication is continuous, recovery instances are not running until needed.

cards.a:
• central backup across services
• tag-based plans
• cross-Region copy

• immutable backups
• WORM
• compliance retention
cards.explanation: WORM = backups cannot be deleted or modified for the lock duration, not even by the AWS root user. Required for compliance retention (HIPAA, SEC, FINRA).

cards.a:
• managed encryption keys
• envelope encryption
• integrated with most AWS services
cards.explanation: Managed encryption key service. Implements envelope encryption: KMS encrypts data keys, and the data keys encrypt the actual data. Integrated with most AWS services (S3 SSE-KMS, EBS, RDS, etc.).

cards.a:
• full control over rotation/disable
• audit via CloudTrail
• you own the key policy
cards.explanation: You own the key policy: who can use the key, which actions, automatic rotation cadence. Required when you need full audit and rotation control (vs AWS-managed keys, which are simpler but opaque).

cards.a:
• keys held outside AWS
• external key manager
• regulatory data sovereignty
cards.explanation: KMS keys backed by an external HSM you operate (third-party vendor, on-prem). The key material never enters AWS. Used when regulation forces key sovereignty.

cards.a:
• DB credentials with auto-rotation
• Lambda rotation function
• native RDS integration
cards.explanation: Stores DB credentials and other secrets, with built-in automatic rotation via Lambda function. Native integration with RDS rotates the password without app changes.

cards.a:
• app config
• secure strings
• no built-in rotation
cards.explanation: Stores app configuration values (and SecureStrings encrypted with KMS). No built-in rotation, simpler and cheaper than Secrets Manager. Use for config; use Secrets Manager for credentials.

cards.a:
• temporary credentials
• EC2/Lambda/ECS access AWS APIs
• cross-account via assume role
cards.explanation: Grants temporary credentials to a principal (EC2, Lambda, ECS task, another account). Replaces long-lived access keys. Cross-account access is done by assuming a role with sts:AssumeRole.

cards.a:
• constrain root user in member accounts
• OU-level allow/deny
• Organizations governance
cards.explanation: Organization-level policy that constrains what any principal in a member account can do, including the root user. The only AWS control that can block actions on the root user of a member account.
tricks: constrain root user in member accounts

cards.a:
• multi-account hierarchy
• consolidated billing
• OUs and SCPs
cards.explanation: Hierarchy of AWS accounts under a management account. Provides consolidated billing, Organizational Units (OUs), and governance via SCPs.

cards.a:
• single sign-on across accounts
• SAML/OIDC federation
• permission sets
cards.explanation: Single sign-on across all your AWS accounts via SAML or OIDC, with permission sets attached to user groups. Replaces the older AWS SSO.

cards.a:
• app user sign-up/sign-in
• user pools and identity pools
• social/SAML federation

• SQL injection / XSS protection
• Layer 7 rules
• attached to ALB/CloudFront/API Gateway
cards.explanation: Web Application Firewall. Layer 7 rules against SQL injection, XSS, bot traffic. Attached to ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, AppSync.

cards.a:
• DDoS protection
• Standard auto-on
• Advanced for 24/7 DRT
cards.explanation: DDoS protection. Standard is on by default and free. Advanced ($3k/mo per org) adds 24/7 access to the DDoS Response Team and cost protection during attacks.

cards.a:
• VPC traffic inspection and filtering
• stateful and stateless rules
• managed firewall
cards.explanation: Managed stateful and stateless firewall for VPC traffic. Replaces legacy on-prem inspection appliances. Suricata-compatible rules.

cards.a:
• central WAF/Shield/Network Firewall policies
• across Organizations
• central enforcement
cards.explanation: Central policy management for WAF rules, Shield Advanced, Network Firewall, Security Groups across accounts in an Organization. Enforces consistent rules everywhere.

cards.a:
• continuous threat detection
• VPC Flow / DNS / CloudTrail logs
• ML-based
cards.explanation: Threat detection on VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, CloudTrail, S3 data events, EKS audit logs. ML detects unusual API calls, port scans, malware C2.

cards.a:
• discover PII in S3
• managed identifiers
• data privacy compliance
cards.explanation: Discovers PII, financial data, and credentials in S3 buckets. Uses ML and managed identifiers (credit card, passport, SSN, etc.). Findings flow to EventBridge or Security Hub.

cards.a:
• EC2/ECR vulnerability scan
• CVE detection
• automated
cards.explanation: Vulnerability scanner for EC2 instances, ECR images, and Lambda functions. Detects CVEs and unintended network exposure.

cards.a:
• API call audit log
• who did what when
• org-wide trail

• resource configuration history
• compliance rules
• drift detection
cards.explanation: Records the configuration of every AWS resource over time. Managed rules detect non-compliance (e.g. unencrypted EBS, public S3 bucket). Auto-remediation via SSM.

cards.a:
• public TLS certificates
• auto-renewal
• DNS validation
cards.explanation: Issues and renews public TLS certificates for free, attached to ALB/CloudFront/API Gateway. DNS validation auto-renews indefinitely. Can also import certs from external CAs.

cards.a:
• maintain N healthy instances
• across multiple AZs
• self-healing
cards.explanation: Maintains a target number of healthy EC2 instances across multiple AZs. Replaces failed instances automatically. Combined with scaling policies for elasticity.

cards.a:
• scale at known time
• predictable peak/off hours
• cron-style

• scale on metrics (CPU, queue depth)
• react to live load
• target tracking

• forecast future load with ML
• historical pattern
• pre-scale before demand
cards.explanation: ML model trained on past CloudWatch metrics forecasts the next 48 hours of load and pre-scales the ASG before demand arrives. Best when load follows daily/weekly patterns.

cards.a:
• metrics, logs, alarms
• operational visibility
• EventBridge integration

• EKS/ECS metrics + logs
• preconfigured dashboards
• container-aware

• analyze cost by service/tag
• 12-month forecast
• filter and granularity

• alert on cost or usage threshold
• monthly/quarterly
• actions on breach
tricks: alert on cost or usage threshold

cards.a:
• ML detects unusual spend
• auto-alert stakeholders
• no rules to write
cards.explanation: ML monitors your AWS spend and alerts on unusual deviations (a service that suddenly costs 10x more, an unexpected workload). No rules to write.

cards.a:
• right-size EC2/EBS/Lambda
• ML recommendations
• cost reduction

• start/stop EC2 and RDS on schedule
• off-hours cost savings
• tag-based
tricks: start/stop EC2 and RDS on schedule

cards.a:
• SQL on S3 directly
• serverless pay-per-query
• ad-hoc analytics
cards.explanation: Serverless SQL query engine that reads data directly from S3. No infrastructure to manage. Pay per TB scanned. Use Glue Data Catalog for schemas.

cards.a:
• serverless ETL
• Spark jobs
• data catalog

• auto-discover schema in S3
• create Glue tables
• feed Athena/Redshift Spectrum
cards.explanation: Automatically detects schemas of files in S3 (CSV, JSON, Parquet) and creates table definitions in the Glue Data Catalog. Athena and Redshift Spectrum then query the tables with SQL.

cards.a:
• managed Hadoop/Spark cluster
• big data parallel processing
• Spot for task nodes

• real-time ingest with shards
• millisecond latency
• custom consumers
cards.explanation: Real-time stream with shards. Each shard handles 1 MB/s write, 2 MB/s read. You manage shards, you write your own consumers.

cards.a:
• managed streaming to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch
• buffering and compression
• no shards
cards.explanation: Fully managed delivery stream that takes data, optionally transforms with Lambda, and writes to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, or Splunk. No shards to manage.

cards.a:
• SQL on streaming data
• real-time analytics
• Apache Flink
cards.explanation: Run SQL or Apache Flink jobs over streaming data from Kinesis Data Streams or Firehose. Used for real-time aggregations, anomaly detection, windowed analytics.

cards.a:
• BI dashboards
• QuickSight users/groups
• ML insights

• data lake governance
• row/cell-level security
• centralized data permissions
cards.explanation: Data lake governance on top of S3 + Glue. Centralizes permissions, supports row-level and cell-level security, audits access. Replaces ad-hoc IAM policies on data.

cards.a:
• build/train/deploy ML
• managed Jupyter
• model hosting

• foundation models as API
• no model training
• GenAI app development
cards.explanation: Access foundation models (Anthropic Claude, Meta Llama, Mistral, Amazon Titan) via API. No model training, no GPU management. Used to build GenAI applications.

cards.a:
• NLP: sentiment, entities, language
• PII detection
• trained model not required
cards.explanation: Pre-trained NLP API: sentiment, key phrase extraction, named entities, language detection, PII detection. No model training needed.

cards.a:
• medical text NLP
• PHI extraction
• ICD-10/RxNorm
cards.explanation: NLP for medical text. Extracts PHI (Protected Health Information), ICD-10 medical codes, RxNorm drug codes from unstructured clinical notes.

cards.a:
• speech to text
• multi-language
• speaker labels

• language translation
• 75+ languages
• real-time API

• extract text from documents
• forms and tables
• PDF/scanned images

• image and video analysis
• face/object/inappropriate content
• moderation
cards.explanation: Pre-trained computer vision API. Detects faces, objects, text, inappropriate content in images and videos. Used for content moderation, identity verification, video analysis.
